newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada budget seen showing more cuts in deficit.
newsitem.headline: Canada budget seen showing more cuts in deficit.

text.p: Canada's Finance Minister Paul Martin will likely deliver more good news about the country's shrinking deficit in his 1997/98 budget on Tuesday, but promise little tax relief or new social spending.

Martin, known for his caution and spending discipline, is expected to exceed the deficit-cutting targets set in his previous budget, something he has achieved since launching his first attack on Canada's huge fiscal gap in 1995.
Martin's fiscal prudence has been instrumental in raising investor confidence in Canada, strengthening the currency and prompting the lowest interest rates in decades.

Few economists believe he will cash in on the good deficit news to to cut taxes or raise government spending, despite pressure from some in his ruling Liberal Party and opposition parties gearing up for an election expected later this year.

"I'm impressed with the progress that's been made to date, but I think it's just a little bit premature to think that you're in a position to spend it," said Andrew Spence, senior economist at brokerage Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Toronto.

Martin has said repeatedly that there was no room for a broad-based tax cut before Canada's books were balanced. He has pledged to eliminate the deficit, but given no time frame. Instead, he has used two-year rolling targets for deficit reduction.
Under the two-year scheme, Martin slashed the deficit to C$28.6 billion ($21.2 billion) in 1995/96 from C$42 billion ($31 billion) in 1994.

In a budget update last October, he repeated his projections for a deficit of C$24.3 billion ($17.9 billion) in 1996/97 and C$17 billion ($12.6 billion) in 1997/98. Canada's fiscal year runs from April through March.

The deficit as a percentage of gross domestic product has dropped to three percent in 1996/97 from 3.7 percent in 1995. It is projected to fall to two percent in 1997/98 and to one percent in 1998/99.

Economists expect Martin to exceed the 1996/97 deficit target by up to C$7 billion ($5.2 billion), bringing the actual deficit down to C$17 billion ($12.6 billion) or C$18 billion ($13.3 billion) instead of the projected C$24.3 billion ($17.9 billion).
But few expect him to admit the full extent of his success in the upcoming budget.

"I don't think he's going to admit to that now. I think he's going to say that it's close to the underlying deficit, which is the C$24.3 (billion) ($17.9 billion) minus C$2.5 billion ($1.9 billion) (from the unused contingency reserve). I think it will probably be around C$20 to C$21 billion ($15.5 billion)," said Patti Croft, chief economist at Canada Trust.
She expected Tuesday's budget to be "a chocolate block full of good news, nicely packaged in a pre-election fashion."
The House of Commons Finance Committee has recommended that Martin stick to his deficit reduction strategy, but also put C$2 billion ($1.5 billion) back into the Canadian economy over several years.
He may also sweeten his budget with some modest tax breaks for charitable donations, trimming employment insurance premiums and a promised attack on child poverty.

"In our view, as long as the stimulus is no larger than this, investor confidence in Paul Martin's commitment to fiscal probity will remain unshaken," David Rosenberg and Douglas Porter, senior economists at brokerage Nesbitt Burns said in a budget preview.
